body_text: Mumbai – July 6, 2026 – TPG, a leading global alternative asset management firm, today announced it has signed definitive agreements to acquire 100 percent stake in Aseem Infrastructure Finance (“Aseem” or the “Company”), alongside co-investor partners GIC and ICICI Bank. ICICI Bank will hold upto 5% in the Company. TPG’s investment is being made through TPG Rise Climate, the firm’s dedicated climate investing platform, as part of its Global South Initiative, a strategy that was launched in partnership with ALTÉRRA and designed to scale climate solutions across emerging markets. Headquartered in Mumbai, Aseem Infrastructure Finance is a leading sustainable infrastructure debt financier with a core focus on renewable energy, power transmission and other infrastructure assets in India. The Company was founded and scaled from inception in 2020 by the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), India’s sovereign-anchored alternative asset manager. NIIF is the Company’s majority shareholder, with the Government of India and SMBC Japan as minority shareholders. To date, Aseem has disbursed over INR 40,000 Cr of loans across critical infrastructure sectors, funding over 27 GW of renewable energy projects, and ~2,000 ckms of power transmission projects, cumulatively abating ~33 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions. “Aseem has been a first-mover in India’s sustainable debt financing space, having built a platform that is uniquely positioned to address the country’s growing climate debt financing needs,” said Sanjeev Mehra, Business Unit Partner at TPG Capital Asia. “We are excited about our investment and look forward to partnering with the management team to be a catalyst through funding climate solutions that drive energy addition and resilience in India, in line with the India government’s target to reach 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030.” Nilesh Shrivastava, Partner, Growth Equity, NIIF said: “Aseem’s growth journey reflects NIIF’s ability to incubate and scale institutional-grade platforms, with strong profitability, governance and asset quality. This transaction underscores growing global investor confidence in India’s sustainable infrastructure and climate financing market. We look forward to Aseem’s continued growth under the stewardship of TPG, GIC and ICICI Bank.” ICICI Securities acted as financial advisor to Aseem and NIIF in connection with the transaction and Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas acted as legal advisors to NIIF. EY acted as the financial advisor and Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas, Linklaters and Trilegal acted as legal advisors to TPG and GIC. The transaction remains subject to customary regulatory approvals and closing conditions. About TPG Rise Climate TPG Rise Climate is the dedicated climate investing platform of TPG, a leading global alternative asset management firm, founded in San Francisco in 1992, with $306 billion of assets under management and investment and operational teams around the world. With dedicated pools of capital across private equity, transition infrastructure, and the Global South, TPG Rise Climate pursues climate-related investments that benefit from the diverse skills of TPG’s investing professionals around the world, the strategic relationships and insights developed across TPG’s broad portfolio of climate companies, and a global network of executives, advisors, and corporate partners. As part of TPG’s $32 billion global impact investing platform, TPG Rise Climate invests broadly across the climate sector, with a focus on building and scaling leading climate solutions across the following thematic areas: clean electrons, clean molecules and materials, and adaptive solutions. For more information, please visit https://www.tpg.com/platforms/impact/rise-climate About National Investment and Infrastructure Fund Limited (NIIF) NIIF is India’s sovereign-anchored alternative asset manager, catalyzing global capital to invest in sectors and asset classes that play an important role in India’s growth journey. Anchored by the Government of India in partnership with leading global investors, NIIF manages USD 5+ billion in equity capital commitments across four strategies — Infrastructure, Private Markets, Growth Equity, and Climate Investments. For more information, please visit www.niifindia.in About GIC GIC is a leading global investment firm established in 1981 to secure Singapore's financial future. As the manager of Singapore's foreign reserves, we take a long-term, disciplined approach to investing. Our asset allocation strategy spans three asset groups — Equities, Fixed Income, and Real Assets. These include investments in developed and emerging market equities, nominal and inflation-linked bonds, private equity, real estate, alternatives, and infrastructure. We are headquartered in Singapore, with a global presence including a talent force of over 2,300 people in 11 key financial cities and investments in over 40 countries. We seek to add meaningful value to our investments and be an investor of choice by leveraging our long-term approach, multi-asset capabilities, and global connectivity. For more information, please visit gic.com.sg About ICICI Bank ICICI Bank Ltd (BSE: ICICIBANK, NSE: ICICIBANK and NYSE:IBN) is a leading private sector bank in India. The Bank’s total assets stood at ₹ 23,72,531 crore at March 31, 2026. For media inquiries, please contact: TPG Edelman India TPG-India@edelman.com NIIF Viraj Nair, Vice President – Corporate Communications viraj.nair@niifindia.in GIC Toh Chuan Ting – Assistant Vice President, Corporate Communications tohchuanting@gic.com.sg

Their platform helps teams and enterprises harness large-scale data to succeed with AI search. For Andrew, AthenaHQ’s founder and CEO, that means treating product development like a scientific process, forming hypotheses from customer insights and validating them rapidly with data. When a scientific culture hits a data bottleneck AthenaHQ’s product questions were clear. Which activation points inside the product predict conversion? Where do users continue to find value over time? Which experiences drive expansion? The friction was in the path from question to answer. Before Julius, answering even basic questions meant pulling an engineer into the room. Engineers had to figure out which tables to query, write SQL, merge results across multiple sources, and repeat that cycle whenever the team learned something new. As Andrew puts it, that work “can get very gnarly very fast.” For Renan, AthenaHQ's evangelist, the pain came from a different angle. "We're querying a database with 7 million rows—it was crazy, things were really slow," he explains. The team tried other solutions: Supabase for querying and plotting helped a little, but Renan still had to manually correlate data points, making the insights "not really useful." He even tried using ChatGPT to help with queries and data analysis, but hit a fundamental limitation: "ChatGPT doesn't have the context of the database. It can't ingest 7 million data rows." The solution: Julius as the data scientist in the room The impact on Renan's workflow was dramatic and measurable. The strategic advantage: speed in a fast-moving market In the rapidly evolving AI search space, speed of learning translates directly to competitive advantage. AthenaHQ's ability to quickly test hypotheses about customer activation, conversion patterns, and value delivery means they can iterate faster than competitors stuck in slower analytical processes. The 7 million rows of citations data—tracking which websites different AI models pull from across various verticals and geographies—represents a goldmine of market intelligence. But that intelligence only matters if it can be extracted quickly enough to inform decisions. In the AI search market where customer expectations and competitive dynamics shift rapidly, this rapid hypothesis testing can mean the difference between leading the market and playing catch-up. What changed for the team Hypotheses tested in hours, not sprints Product managers can validate activation hypotheses quickly without waiting for engineering bandwidth. title: Top 2 strategies to secure investment for AI-powered asset optimization in manufacturing
summary: As a manufacturing manager, you likely face the challenge of navigating a crowded field of investment proposals. Often, more tangible projects—such as upgrading a production line—take precedence because their benefits are easier to grasp.
body_text: Top 2 strategies to secure investment for AI-powered asset optimization in manufacturing Asset optimization initiatives across industries Complexity of decision-making in investment optimization What are some of the real-world implementation challenges? Strategies to move forward with asset performance optimization Taking a strategic approach to asset maintenance investment As a manufacturing manager, you likely face the challenge of navigating a crowded field of investment proposals. Often, more tangible projects—such as upgrading a production line—take precedence because their benefits are easier to grasp. So, how can you overcome this challenge and secure funding for asset maintenance improvements? In this blog, I share proven strategies to help you gain approval for your proposals and secure the resources you need. Asset optimization initiatives across industries Asset optimization initiatives vary widely depending on the industry, the type of equipment, and the specific goals of the business. These initiatives are designed to improve efficiency, reduce costs and enhance the overall reliability of critical assets. Let's look at examples from different manufacturing sectors to illustrate diverse approaches. Optimizing wear predictions in polyethylene (pe) production: A large polyethylene (PE) producer wants to optimize the wear patterns of knife edges used to cut endless PE strands into small granules. The challenge here is striking the right balance: repair too early, and the costs increase unnecessarily; repair too late, and the product quality suffers due to degraded cutting precision. The use of predictive maintenance techniques can assist with this. Rail switch monitoring for national railway operators: A national railway operator uses an asset monitoring and management system for real-time health status updates for 6,000 rail switches and wants to enhance the system’s capabilities by incorporating predictive features. Specifically, the focus is on predicting Remaining Useful Life (RUL) and failure modes for rail switches. Deeper insights into the performance trends and potential failure scenarios can help plan maintenance more effectively, reduce unexpected repairs, and ultimately extend the Mean Time Between Repairs (MTBR), while optimizing costs and improving safety. Improving product quality and maintenance in foam manufacturing: High-end foam is made in vertical ovens, with heating pads to roll sheets of foam into delicate, thin foam rolls. When one of these pads fails, the issue is not immediately visible. However, the product quality deteriorates, impacting production efficiency and product consistency. Monitoring the heating pads' health in real time requires sensors and asset monitoring technology. Furthermore, incorporating predictive analytics can help estimate the components' RUL, allowing for more timely repairs. Complexity of decision-making in investment optimization In the latest CGI Voice of Our Clients research, 38% of manufacturing executives identify optimizing investments and operations as a significant challenge in achieving better outcomes. The complexity of optimizing an investment portfolio can be attributed to several factors, particularly the fast-evolving technology landscape. A major challenge for manufacturers is the sheer volume of new technology providers emerging with solutions that could potentially revolutionize operations. Some examples are: Cloud solutions disrupting traditional systems The rise of cloud technology has made solutions from hyperscalers viable alternatives to traditional Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) and Computerized Maintenance Management Systems (CMMS). These cloud providers now play an increasingly significant role in the Manufacturing Operations Management Systems (MOMS) landscape, offering scalability and flexibility that traditional on-premise solutions struggle to match. Data and analytics platforms are the new norm With the surge in data generation, many existing MES providers and new market entrants are developing dedicated platforms for managing production data and providing AI-driven insights. These platforms offer robust functionality and sophisticated self-service capabilities that allow manufacturers to harness data in real time, enhancing decision-making and operational effectiveness performance. Emergence of self-service and low-code solutions The increasing use of self-service and low-code platforms—designed for production environments—enables manufacturers to develop tailored workflows and automate processes without requiring extensive technical expertise. This democratization of software development facilitates quicker implementation and more agile responses to evolving operational needs. Evolution of MES/MOMS Traditional MES vendors are broadening their offerings to encompass the entire range of MOMS with integrated capabilities that now feature AI tools customized for specific use cases. This evolution allows manufacturers to access more comprehensive solutions that unify various operational aspects, from real-time monitoring to predictive maintenance. AI: from hype to reality Manufacturers are moving beyond theoretical applications of AI and even generative AI (GenAI) to prioritize tangible, use-case-driven deployments. The availability of AI-based solutions that are not just aspirational but scalable offers measurable improvements in production efficiency, predictive maintenance, quality control, and more. What are some of the real-world implementation challenges? CMMS/EAM investments frequently compete with projects that provide quicker, more tangible returns, such as new machinery or product development. While these options may seem more beneficial in the short term, effective implementation of CMMS/EAM ultimately enhances asset availability, production quality, operational efficiency, and long-term profitability. High initial costs : Smaller manufacturers are often discouraged by the significant upfront investment required to implement a CMMS/EAM system, which includes software licensing, integration, and hardware infrastructure. Additionally, the total cost of ownership can increase notably due to customizations, system upgrades, and the incorporation of hardware such as sensors and IoT devices. Integration complexity : Data inconsistencies, legacy systems, and siloed data across departments can make the integration of a CMMS/EAM system with other enterprise systems such as ERP, inventory, and IoT platforms complex and costly. Additionally, the integration process can lead to operational disruptions that need to be managed carefully. Lack of skilled personnel : Operating modern CMMS/EAM solutions requires expertise in areas like data analytics, IoT, and IT management, which manufacturers currently lack. Added to that, maintenance teams accustomed to traditional, manual methods may resist transitioning to digital CMMS/EAM systems, necessitating investments in change management, training and fostering a culture of digital adoption. Data quality and availability issues : Inconsistent or outdated data on machine conditions, maintenance histories, and asset life cycles can severely limit the effectiveness of a CMMS/EAM system. For a CMMS/EAM system to deliver maximum value, data must be standardized across all machines and assets. However, inconsistent data formats across different departments or sites can complicate data integration and reduce system efficiency, requiring significant effort in data cleansing and standardization. Cybersecurity concerns : Manufacturers worry that CMMS/EAM systems, if not properly secured, could expose them to cyber threats, potentially endangering sensitive operational data and asset integrity. Furthermore, fulfilling cybersecurity and data protection compliance requirements can be complex and resource-intensive. Difficulty in demonstrating ROI : Companies often face a learning curve and need time to fully realize the benefits of these systems, making it harder to quantify ROI quickly. Additionally, measuring value adds further complexity. Quantifying asset availability and performance improvements—such as reduced downtime or increased product quality—requires detailed analysis, which can be difficult to achieve in the short term. Strategies to move forward with asset performance optimization Securing your budget for asset maintenance and optimization requires a strategic approach that aligns your efforts with broader organizational goals while emphasizing the full range of benefits that asset optimization can provide. Strategy 1: Seek synergies with other digital transformation initiatives When executives prioritize investment proposals, they typically align them with key company drivers or strategic objectives. Asset optimization initiatives are often internally promoted primarily based on their impact on maintenance costs. While this alone is usually sufficient to justify a healthy ROI, securing the necessary budget often requires demonstrating additional, broader benefits. Try to identify synergies between asset management efforts and other strategic objectives, which typically could range from sustainability and cost reduction to supply chain agility, production quality, product safety, and environmental, health and safety (EHS) compliance. This holistic approach can create efficiencies and drive greater returns on investment, making it easier to secure the necessary budget for future initiatives. Strategy 2: Demonstrate benefits beyond asset availability Beyond maintenance savings, asset optimization drives significant reductions in production costs. With improved machine reliability and more predictable availability, manufacturers can schedule production more efficiently and achieve higher overall equipment effectiveness (OEE). Asset optimization also reduces waste. With proactive monitoring, unexpected breakdowns can be anticipated and prevented, minimizing product loss and maximizing yield. Furthermore, asset optimization leads to higher-quality production. By ensuring machines operate at peak performance, closer to their optimal settings, manufacturers can achieve tighter tolerances and more consistent product quality. Taking a strategic approach to asset maintenance investment Securing investment for asset maintenance and optimization can be challenging, but it is far from impossible. By integrating your proposal with larger digital initiatives and quantifying the broader business outcomes, you can present a compelling case for your asset maintenance strategy. Such a strategic approach that aligns your goals with the business’ priorities will ensure your plant’s assets are running at peak efficiency while also securing the necessary resources to drive long-term success. title: FedEx Opens New World Service Center in Cebu to Power Regional Trade Connectivity
body_text: FedEx Philippines marks the opening of its new World Service Center in Cebu, enhancing its presence in Visayas and providing businesses and individuals with more convenient access to customs support and international shipping services. (From left to right: Anne Marie Liwag-Inawat, Senior Manager for Sales, Maribeth Espinosa, Managing Director, and Raymond Morales, Operations Manager) Cebu, Philippines, July 27, 2026 – Federal Express Corporation (FedEx), one of the world’s largest express transportation companies, has opened a new World Service Center in Lapu-Lapu City, Cebu, further strengthening its network in the Visayas region and enhancing support for businesses engaged in international trade. Located at the Ground-Air Logistics Corporation (GALCO) Complex, 2nd Floor, Unit 3, within the Mactan-Cebu International Airport Cargo Complex and adjacent to the Bureau of Customs (BOC) Cebu office, the new facility is strategically positioned to streamline customs clearance. On-site clearance processors are available to assist customers with customs-related inquiries and documentation requirements at the World Service Center. In addition, the facility serves as a convenient shipment drop-off location, providing greater flexibility for businesses and individuals seeking access to FedEx services without scheduling a pickup. “As Cebu continues to strengthen its position as a major hub for trade, manufacturing, and entrepreneurship, FedEx remains committed to investing in infrastructure that helps local businesses connect with global opportunities,” said Maribeth Espinosa, managing director, FedEx Philippines. “The Cebu World Service Center brings our services closer to customers, making international shipping more accessible, efficient, and convenient. From established exporters to growing small and medium enterprises, customers can rely on FedEx for the expertise, connectivity, and support they need to expand beyond borders and unlock new growth opportunities.” The new facility complements FedEx’s existing air network in Cebu, which includes six inbound flights weekly (Sunday through Friday) and five outbound flights weekly (Monday through Thursday and Saturday). Together, these investments enhance the company’s operational capabilities in the Visayas, enabling businesses in Cebu and neighboring provinces to benefit from faster, more seamless access to more than 220 countries and territories through the FedEx global network. As cross-border e-commerce and regional trade continue to accelerate, the Cebu World Service Center underscores the company’s commitment to strengthening logistics infrastructure in key growth markets across the Philippines. title: Apa Itu Diaspora Indonesia? Makna, Peran, dan Faktanya
summary: Apa itu diaspora Indonesia? Pelajari makna, siapa saja yang termasuk, peran mereka bagi negara, dan fakta menarik seputar komunitas diaspora di seluruh dunia.
body_text: Pernahkah kamu bertemu seseorang di luar negeri, lalu ternyata dia orang Indonesia juga? Rasanya seperti menemukan saudara jauh di tengah kota asing. Dari London sampai Tokyo, dari Sydney sampai Dubai, orang Indonesia ada di mana-mana. Mereka belajar, bekerja, membangun keluarga, bahkan menetap puluhan tahun di negeri orang. Nah, kelompok inilah yang sering disebut sebagai diaspora Indonesia . Tapi sebenarnya, apa itu diaspora Indonesia? Siapa saja yang masuk kategori ini, dan seberapa besar peran mereka bagi Indonesia? Kalau kamu penasaran, atau bahkan merasa kamu bagian dari mereka, artikel ini wajib kamu baca sampai habis. Kamu juga bisa mulai dari panduan cara kerja di luar negeri kalau ingin memahami konteks lebih luas. Daftar Isi Toggle Apa Itu Diaspora Indonesia? Secara sederhana, diaspora Indonesia adalah seluruh orang Indonesia, baik warga negara Indonesia (WNI) maupun keturunan Indonesia, yang tinggal dan menetap di luar negeri. Mereka bisa berstatus pelajar, pekerja profesional, tenaga kerja, hingga warga negara asing keturunan Indonesia. Kata diaspora sendiri berasal dari bahasa Yunani, yang berarti “penyebaran” atau “tercerai-berai”. Dalam konteks modern, istilah ini merujuk pada komunitas suatu bangsa yang hidup di luar batas negaranya, namun tetap memiliki ikatan kuat dengan tanah asal. 1. Siapa Saja yang Termasuk Diaspora Indonesia? Tidak semua orang Indonesia di luar negeri otomatis disebut diaspora. Ada beberapa kategori yang biasanya masuk dalam definisi ini: WNI yang bekerja di luar negeri , baik sebagai profesional, tenaga ahli, maupun pekerja migran. Pelajar dan mahasiswa Indonesia yang menempuh studi di universitas luar negeri. WNI yang menikah dengan warga negara asing dan menetap di negara pasangannya. Keturunan Indonesia yang lahir di luar negeri namun masih memiliki darah atau identitas budaya Indonesia. Mantan WNI yang telah berganti kewarganegaraan tapi tetap merasa terikat secara kultural dengan Indonesia. 2. Berapa Jumlah Diaspora Indonesia di Dunia? Angkanya sangat besar. Indonesia masuk dalam daftar negara dengan jumlah diaspora terbanyak di dunia. Jutaan orang Indonesia tersebar di berbagai penjuru dunia, dari Asia Tenggara, Timur Tengah, Australia, Eropa, Amerika, hingga Afrika. Malaysia menjadi salah satu negara dengan komunitas diaspora Indonesia terbesar, diikuti Arab Saudi, Belanda, Amerika Serikat, dan Australia. Ini bukan angka kecil, ini sebuah kekuatan yang, jika dikelola dengan baik, bisa memberi dampak luar biasa bagi Indonesia. Mengapa Orang Indonesia Memilih Tinggal di Luar Negeri? Motivasi setiap orang berbeda-beda. Tidak ada satu alasan tunggal yang menjelaskan mengapa seseorang memilih hidup di luar negeri dalam jangka panjang. 1. Peluang Karier dan Pendapatan Lebih Baik Banyak profesional Indonesia yang tertarik dengan pasar kerja internasional karena menawarkan gaji, fasilitas, dan jenjang karier yang kompetitif. Kalau kamu ingin mendalami topik ini lebih lanjut, ada panduan lengkap tentang bekerja sebagai profesional Indonesia di Malaysia yang bisa jadi referensi bagus. 2. Pendidikan Berkualitas Tinggi Universitas-universitas di luar negeri, terutama di Eropa, Amerika, dan Australia, menjadi magnet bagi pelajar Indonesia yang ingin mendapatkan gelar dan pengalaman kelas dunia. Banyak dari mereka yang akhirnya menetap setelah lulus karena mendapat tawaran kerja. 3. Ikatan Keluarga atau Pernikahan Tidak sedikit orang Indonesia yang awalnya hanya ikut pasangan, tapi akhirnya membangun kehidupan penuh di sana. Ini adalah salah satu jalur paling organik terbentuknya diaspora. 4. Iklim, Gaya Hidup, dan Alasan Pribadi Ada juga yang memilih tinggal di luar negeri karena alasan yang lebih personal, mulai dari iklim yang lebih sesuai kondisi kesehatan, kebebasan berekspresi, hingga sekadar jatuh cinta dengan negara tertentu. Peran Diaspora Indonesia bagi Tanah Air Ini bagian yang paling menarik. Diaspora Indonesia bukan sekadar “orang yang pergi”, mereka justru bisa menjadi salah satu aset terbesar bagi kemajuan Indonesia. 1. Remitansi: Aliran Dana dari Luar Negeri ke Indonesia Setiap bulan, jutaan diaspora Indonesia mengirimkan uang ke keluarga mereka di tanah air. Dalam skala makro, aliran dana ini, yang disebut remitansi , menjadi salah satu sumber devisa penting bagi Indonesia. Bagi yang ingin mengirim uang untuk investasi properti di Indonesia , ini juga jadi bagian dari kontribusi nyata diaspora. 2. Transfer Ilmu dan Teknologi Diaspora yang bekerja di sektor teknologi, riset, dan pendidikan di luar negeri membawa pulang pengetahuan berharga ketika mereka kembali ke Indonesia, atau berbagi ilmu dari jauh melalui kolaborasi lintas negara. 3. Mempromosikan Budaya Indonesia di Dunia Dari festival kuliner hingga pertunjukan tari tradisional, diaspora Indonesia aktif memperkenalkan budaya Indonesia kepada dunia. Mereka adalah duta budaya yang tidak resmi, tapi dampaknya sangat nyata. 4. Jaringan Bisnis Internasional Banyak diaspora yang membangun jembatan bisnis antara Indonesia dengan negara tempat mereka tinggal. Mereka memahami dua budaya sekaligus, yang menjadikan mereka negosiator dan penghubung yang sangat efektif. Tantangan yang Dihadapi Diaspora Indonesia Hidup di luar negeri tidak selalu mudah. Ada banyak tantangan yang harus dihadapi oleh diaspora Indonesia setiap harinya. 1. Kerinduan dan Identitas Budaya Tinggal jauh dari keluarga dan tanah air bisa memunculkan rasa rindu yang dalam. Mempertahankan identitas sebagai orang Indonesia di tengah budaya asing juga bukan hal yang mudah, terutama bagi generasi kedua. 2. Mengelola Keuangan Lintas Negara Mengatur keuangan di dua negara sekaligus, mengirim uang ke Indonesia, berinvestasi, sekaligus memenuhi kebutuhan hidup di luar negeri, adalah tantangan tersendiri. Artikel tentang tips mengatur keuangan untuk diaspora Indonesia di Malaysia bisa jadi panduan yang sangat praktis. 3. Adaptasi Hukum dan Administrasi Setiap negara punya aturan yang berbeda, soal visa, pajak, hingga status kewarganegaraan. Memahami aturan-aturan ini butuh waktu dan energi yang tidak sedikit. Beberapa diaspora bahkan harus mempertimbangkan proses seperti naturalisasi , yang bisa kamu pelajari lebih lanjut di artikel apa itu naturalisasi . Cara Diaspora Indonesia Tetap Terhubung dengan Tanah Air Meski jauh, ikatan dengan Indonesia tidak pernah benar-benar putus. Ada banyak cara yang dilakukan diaspora untuk tetap dekat dengan akar mereka: Bergabung dengan komunitas dan organisasi diaspora Indonesia di luar negeri. Memasak makanan Indonesia dan merayakan hari besar nasional bersama komunitas. Mengajarkan bahasa Indonesia kepada anak-anak mereka yang lahir di luar negeri. Rutin mengikuti berita dan perkembangan di Indonesia lewat media digital. Mengirim uang secara rutin kepada keluarga di Indonesia melalui layanan remitansi yang mudah dan terpercaya seperti Transfez. Baca Juga: Bagaimana Cara Kerja di Luar Negeri: Panduan Lengkap Menjadi bagian dari diaspora Indonesia bukan berarti meninggalkan identitas, justru sebaliknya. Mereka adalah bukti bahwa semangat Indonesia bisa tumbuh dan bersinar di mana saja di dunia. Kalau kamu salah satunya, atau sedang mempertimbangkan untuk melangkah lebih jauh ke luar negeri, ingatlah bahwa komunitas ini selalu ada untuk saling mendukung. Dan kalau kamu perlu cara mudah mengirim uang ke keluarga di Indonesia, Transfez hadir sebagai solusi yang simpel untuk memastikan orang-orang yang kamu sayangi tetap terjaga, ke mana pun langkahmu membawa pergi. title: How to Write Career Center Newsletters Students Actually Open
summary: A practical guide for career centers on writing student newsletters with clearer subject lines, a consistent cadence, focused content, mobile-friendly formatting, and targeted calls to action.
body_text: How should career centers write newsletters students actually open? Career centers should write student newsletters by making the value clear within seconds. Each issue should have a defined audience, a specific action goal, a descriptive subject line, a useful preheader, a consistent cadence, and a focused content mix students can scan quickly on mobile. Strong newsletters lead with the most relevant opportunity, include a small selection of jobs or internships, add one manageable career action, promote one upcoming event, and close with one accessible support option. The goal is not to include every announcement. It is to help students quickly understand what is relevant, what needs action soon, and where to go next. If your career center already sends a student newsletter but open rates, clicks, and event registrations remain low, the problem may be the way the newsletter is packaged. Students need to understand within seconds why the email is relevant, what deserves their attention, and what they should do next. A useful career newsletter does not need elaborate graphics or a long list of announcements. It needs a clear subject line, a predictable cadence, a focused content mix, and a format students can scan quickly between classes. This guide explains how to structure each issue, write subject lines around student priorities, select an appropriate sending schedule, and decide which opportunities deserve space in the email. What Should Career Centers Decide Before Writing the Newsletter? Career centers should decide who the newsletter is for and what action it should prompt before collecting content. An email written for “all students” can quickly become a long list of unrelated jobs, events, articles, and reminders. Use the following standards as a starting point: Newsletter element Practical standard Primary audience One student group or a clearly defined general audience Subject line The most useful or time-sensitive item in the issue Lead story One opportunity that deserves immediate attention Supporting content Three to five short, distinct content blocks Primary action One prominent next step, such as register, apply, book, or prepare Reading time Easy to scan and act on within two minutes Before adding an item, ask whether it helps the intended student audience make a career-related decision or complete a useful action. An announcement that does not meet either standard may belong in another communication channel. The finished newsletter should answer three questions immediately: Is this information relevant to me? Is there anything I need to act on soon? Where do I go to complete the next step? How Should Career Centers Write Newsletter Subject Lines? Career center newsletter subject lines should identify the strongest reason to open the email. Students should be able to tell whether the edition contains an application deadline, career fair, workshop, employer event, or practical resource before opening it. Mailchimp recommends keeping subject lines descriptive, audience-aware, and short enough to display clearly on mobile devices. Its guidance suggests using no more than nine words and 60 characters as a practical limit, while testing different versions to learn what the specific audience responds to. Lead With the Opportunity, Benefit, or Deadline Useful subject lines communicate what students can gain or what they may miss. Examples include: 5 internships closing this Friday Meet 40 employers at Thursday’s career fair First-years: Explore careers connected to your major Free professional headshots available Wednesday Seniors: Prepare your resume before recruiting begins Marketing roles hiring this week Three steps to prepare for next week’s interviews The strongest subject line will usually come from the lead item rather than the newsletter’s internal name. Avoid Generic Newsletter Labels Labels such as these provide little information: Career Center Newsletter This Week at the Career Center October Career Update Opportunities and Resources Important Career Information A recurring newsletter name can appear after the useful information: 6 internships closing soon | Career Center Weekly Prepare for the fall career fair | Career Center Update Graduate roles hiring now | Friday Career Brief This preserves a recognizable series name while placing the student-facing value first. Use Specificity Before Wordplay The University of Dallas Office of Personal Career Development previously tested catchy and pun-based subject lines. Student feedback showed that recipients wanted to know what an email contained before opening it, so the team shifted toward clearer, more specific subject lines. According to NACE’s profile of the University of Dallas email strategy , the office reported average open rates between 60% and 80%, with results varying by topic and student audience. The team also tailored subject lines and greetings for groups such as first-year students, upper-level students, and graduate students. The lesson is straightforward: students should understand the subject before they encounter the creativity. Use the Preheader to Add a Second Reason to Open The preheader is the short preview text that appears beside or below the subject line in many inboxes. It should add information instead of repeating the subject. Mailchimp describes the preheader as one of the first elements recipients see when deciding whether to open an email. Its guidance recommends using the space to summarize the content, explain the benefit, or signal the next action. For example: Subject: 5 internships closing this Friday Preheader: Plus resume drop-ins and two employer events next week. Subject: First-years: Explore careers connected to your major Preheader: Start with three activities that take less than 20 minutes. Subject: Prepare for Thursday’s engineering fair Preheader: Review the employer list and bring your resume for feedback. How Often Should Career Centers Send a Student Newsletter? The newsletter should follow a cadence the career center can maintain and students can recognize. Weekly and biweekly schedules both work within a career services context, depending on how quickly the available opportunities change and how narrowly the content is targeted. Use a Weekly Cadence for Frequently Changing Opportunities A weekly newsletter may be appropriate when the career center regularly has: New jobs and internships Employer information sessions Career fairs and workshops Application deadlines Appointment availability Time-sensitive preparation guidance Send the main newsletter on a consistent day rather than selecting a new time for every edition. The University of Dallas Office of Personal Career Development sends its main student email every Sunday night. The team selected the schedule after experimenting with different days and times, then maintained it so students would know when to expect the weekly message. The precise day will depend on the institution. Consistency should follow testing rather than assumption. Use a Biweekly Cadence for More Targeted Content A biweekly newsletter may suit career centers that organize communications by industry, career interest, school, or broad major group. The additional time between editions allows the team to curate a smaller collection of relevant opportunities. UC Santa Cruz Career Success sends industry-community newsletter updates every two weeks. Students can select communities aligned with their interests and receive targeted events, jobs, and industry guidance. A career center could use this structure for groups such as: Arts, media, and communications Business and entrepreneurship Engineering and technology Environment and sustainability Government and public service Science and healthcare The newsletter does not need to become more frequent simply because more content is available. The priority is a dependable flow of relevant information. Reserve One-Off Emails for Genuine Urgency Extra emails should be sent when waiting for the next scheduled newsletter would reduce the value of the information. Appropriate reasons may include: An application deadline within the next few days A newly added employer event A location or schedule change Additional career fair capacity An opportunity available only to a specific student group One-off messages should be narrowly targeted. Sending every general announcement separately makes it harder for students to distinguish urgent messages from routine promotion. What Content Mix Gives Students a Reason to Open Each Edition? Each newsletter should combine immediate opportunities with practical career support. Jobs and events provide urgency, while preparation activities make the email useful to students who are not ready to apply or attend. A focused edition can contain five elements: 1. One Lead Opportunity Select the most useful or time-sensitive item and place it at the top. A lead block should include: What the opportunity is Who it is for Why it may be useful The relevant date or deadline One direct action For example: Applications close Friday: Paid sustainability internships Three local organizations are recruiting students from all majors for summer positions. Review the requirements and submit your application by 5 p.m. Friday. View the internships The description gives students enough information to decide whether to click without requiring a long introduction. 2. A Small Selection of Jobs or Internships Avoid reproducing the entire job board in the newsletter. Select a manageable number of opportunities and label them according to the information students need. Useful labels may include: Open to all majors No previous experience required Paid summer internship On-campus position Suitable for first-year students Application closes this week An archived UMBC Career Center newsletter for STEM majors led with new internships and jobs for science students, then directed readers to appointments, programs, and related career resources. The edition presented a sample of relevant roles rather than treating the email as a substitute for the full opportunity database. 3. One Manageable Career Action Students who are not ready to apply for a position or attend an event should still find something useful to complete. Examples include: Add one quantified result to your resume Save three employers attending the career fair Complete a short career interest assessment Practise one common interview question Update your LinkedIn headline Book a resume review Identify one alumnus to contact Link the action directly to the relevant resource, appointment page, or career platform. Avoid making students search the career center website after clicking. 4. One Upcoming Event Include only the details needed to make a decision: Event title Date and time Intended audience Purpose Registration link For example: Healthcare Employer Panel Tuesday, October 14, 4 p.m. Hear from recruiters in public health, clinical research, and healthcare administration. Open to students from all majors. Register for the panel 5. One Support Option Close the content mix with one accessible form of support, such as: Drop-in advising hours Appointment availability Resume or interview preparation Career exploration resources A job-search guide A career technology tool The support option should connect naturally to the other content. An edition promoting a career fair might end with resume feedback or employer-research guidance. How Should a Career Center Newsletter Be Formatted? A career center newsletter should be easy to scan on a phone. Use short content blocks, descriptive headings, visible deadlines, meaningful links, and a clear order of importance. Mailchimp recommends concise newsletter copy, a clear call to action, and an inverted-pyramid structure that places the strongest message first. A practical format includes the following elements. Use a Recognizable Sender Name Students should immediately recognize the sender. Clear options include: State University Career Center College of Business Career Services Jordan from the Career Center Avoid unexplained office abbreviations, staff initials, and system-generated names. Open With a One-Sentence Summary The first sentence should tell students what the edition contains. For example: This week’s update includes five paid internships closing soon, preparation for the spring career fair, and new resume drop-in times. Long greetings, office updates, and general introductions delay the information students opened the email to find. Place One Prominent Item First The first content block should receive the strongest headline, clearest explanation, and most visible call to action. Secondary items can follow in shorter blocks. Use a consistent pattern for each: Descriptive heading One or two sentences explaining the opportunity and relevant deadline. Specific action link Use Meaningful Link Text Link text should tell the student what will happen after clicking. Use: View the internship requirements Register for the career fair Book a resume review Explore interview practice See participating employers Avoid: Click here Learn more Read more Go Mailchimp’s email accessibility guidance recommends meaningful link text, logical headings, responsive structure, alt text, and keeping essential information out of images. Keep the Mobile Layout Simple Use a single-column layout whenever possible. Multiple columns may stack unpredictably on smaller screens and can disrupt the intended reading order. Keep paragraphs short, use buttons large enough to tap, and check that dates and deadlines remain visible without zooming. Test the newsletter on several screen sizes before sending it to the full list. End With a Functional Footer The footer should include: Career center name Contact information Office location Accessibility information where applicable Subscription preferences Required email-management links Avoid using the footer as another section for announcements. Should Career Centers Send the Same Newsletter to Every Student? Career centers should segment newsletters when the usefulness of the content changes substantially between student groups. Start with a few stable categories, then use a student persona messaging playbook to adjust the subject line, lead item, tone, and call to action for each group. Useful segments may include: Class year Undergraduate and graduate students Academic school or broad major group Career interest or industry International students Students searching for internships Students approaching graduation Yale College allows students to customize its weekly Office of Career Strategy newsletter according to their interests. The selected preferences determine the job postings, internship opportunities, events, blogs, and resources students receive. The University of Denver describes a preference structure with two levels : the type of content, such as jobs, events, blogs, and resources, and the area of interest, such as an academic category or industry. A smaller career center can apply the same principle without building a complex preference system: Send one general newsletter and change the lead block by class year, including a distinct approach to engaging first-year students in career planning . Create separate editions during major recruiting periods. Send industry-focused newsletters every two weeks. Target event reminders to registered or interested students. Adjust the subject line for each student segment. Feature graduate opportunities only in the graduate edition. Even limited segmentation can remove content that has no practical relevance for the recipient. How Can Career Centers Evaluate Newsletter Performance? Career centers should evaluate whether students complete the intended actions after receiving the newsletter. Open rates help assess subject lines and sender recognition, while clicks, registrations, attendance, and appointments show whether the content prompted meaningful engagement. Track measures such as: Open rate Click rate Clicks on the lead item Event registrations Event attendance Appointment requests Job and internship link clicks Resource or career platform usage Replies from students Unsubscribes Results by student segment The University of Dallas career team reviews click rates, event RSVPs, attendance, appointment requests, and direct emails alongside its open rates. Staff reported seeing increases in advising requests and event registrations after some messages were sent. Review several editions before changing the entire newsletter. Test one major variable at a time. For example: Compare a specific subject line with a general one. Test two sending times while keeping the content unchanged. Move the primary action higher in the email. Compare general and segmented versions. Reduce the number of content blocks. Replace vague link text with specific actions. Career centers should also ask students directly which sections they use, which information feels repetitive, and what makes an email worth opening. A small student review group can identify problems that email-platform metrics do not explain. Wrapping Up A strong newsletter should do more than promote opportunities. It should guide students toward a clear next step, whether that means exploring career options, improving a resume, preparing for an interview, or strengthening a LinkedIn profile. Hiration gives career centers a full-stack career readiness suite that supports those actions across the student journey. Students can access Career Assessments and AI-powered modules for Resume Optimization, Interview Simulation, LinkedIn optimization, and other career preparation activities. Career teams can use the separate Counselor Module to manage cohorts, workflows, student progress, and analytics within a secure, FERPA and SOC 2-compliant platform. This gives each newsletter a clearer destination and helps career teams connect student outreach with measurable career readiness activity. Career Center Newsletters — FAQs How should career centers write newsletters students actually open? Career centers should write newsletters that quickly show relevance, urgency, and the next action. Each issue should use a clear subject line, a focused lead item, short content blocks, meaningful links, mobile-friendly formatting, and a predictable cadence students can recognize. What should career centers decide before writing a newsletter? Career centers should decide who the newsletter is for, what student action it should prompt, which content deserves space, and what the reader should understand within the first few seconds. This prevents the email from becoming a long list of unrelated announcements. What should a student career newsletter answer immediately? A student career newsletter should answer three questions immediately: whether the information is relevant to the student, whether anything needs action soon, and where the student should go to complete the next step. How should career centers write newsletter subject lines? Career center newsletter subject lines should identify the strongest reason to open the email, such as an application deadline, career fair, employer event, workshop, resource, or student benefit. The subject line should be specific, descriptive, and short enough to display clearly on mobile. What are good career center newsletter subject line examples? Strong examples include “5 internships closing this Friday,” “Meet 40 employers at Thursday’s career fair,” “First-years: Explore careers connected to your major,” “Free professional headshots available Wednesday,” and “Prepare for the fall career fair.” What subject lines should career centers avoid? Career centers should avoid vague labels such as “Career Center Newsletter,” “This Week at the Career Center,” “October Career Update,” “Opportunities and Resources,” or “Important Career Information” because they do not tell students what the email contains. How should career centers use newsletter preheaders? The preheader should add a second reason to open the email instead of repeating the subject line. It can summarize the issue, mention another useful item, explain the benefit, or point to the next action students can take. How often should career centers send a student newsletter? Career centers should use a cadence they can maintain and students can recognize. Weekly newsletters work well when jobs, internships, events, and deadlines change frequently. Biweekly newsletters may work better for targeted industry, school, major, or student-interest editions. When should career centers send one-off student emails? One-off emails should be reserved for genuine urgency, such as an application deadline within a few days, a newly added employer event, a location or schedule change, additional career fair capacity, or an opportunity available only to a specific student group. What content mix works best in a career center newsletter? A focused newsletter can include one lead opportunity, a small selection of jobs or internships, one manageable career action, one upcoming event, and one support option such as advising, resume review, interview preparation, career exploration, or a career platform. How many jobs or internships should a newsletter include? A newsletter should include a small, curated selection rather than reproduce the entire job board. Opportunities should be labeled clearly with useful details such as “open to all majors,” “paid summer internship,” “no previous experience required,” or “application closes this week.” What career actions can newsletters ask students to complete? Useful newsletter actions include adding one quantified result to a resume, saving three employers attending a career fair, completing a career interest assessment, practicing one interview question, updating a LinkedIn headline, booking a resume review, or identifying one alumnus to contact. How should a career center newsletter be formatted? A career center newsletter should be easy to scan on a phone. Use a recognizable sender name, a one-sentence opening summary, one prominent lead item, short secondary blocks, clear deadlines, meaningful link text, a simple single-column layout, and a functional footer. What link text should career centers use in newsletters? Link text should describe the action students will take after clicking. Use phrases such as “View the internship requirements,” “Register for the career fair,” “Book a resume review,” “Explore interview practice,” or “See participating employers” instead of vague text like “click here” or “learn more.” Should career centers send the same newsletter to every student? Career centers should segment newsletters when the usefulness of the content changes by class year, academic school, major group, career interest, student status, or job-search stage. Even limited segmentation can remove irrelevant content and make each issue more useful to the recipient. What student segments work well for career newsletters? Useful segments include first-year students, upper-level students, graduate students, academic schools, broad major groups, industry interests, international students, students searching for internships, and students approaching graduation. How can career centers evaluate newsletter performance? Career centers should evaluate whether students complete the intended actions after receiving the newsletter. Useful metrics include open rate, click rate, clicks on the lead item, event registrations, event attendance, appointment requests, job and internship link clicks, replies, unsubscribes, and results by student segment. Why are open rates not enough to measure newsletter success? Open rates help assess subject lines and sender recognition, but they do not show whether the email produced meaningful engagement. Career centers should also track clicks, registrations, attendance, appointments, resource usage, replies, and whether students completed the intended next step. How can career centers improve student newsletter performance over time? Career centers should test one major variable at a time, such as subject line specificity, sending time, lead item placement, segmentation, number of content blocks, or link text. They should also ask students directly which sections they use and what makes an email worth opening. How can Hiration support student newsletter engagement? Hiration can give each newsletter a clearer destination by supporting student actions across career assessments, resume optimization, interview simulation, LinkedIn optimization, and other career preparation activities. title: A Foundational Piece of Insurance Modernization You Can’t Afford to Overlook? Documents.
summary: In our recent Marketplace Conversations webinar with GhostDraft and MEMIC, industry leaders explored a significant shift shaping organizations today
body_text: Home Resources Resources Download Center Guidewire Conversations Podcasts Blog Help and Support Insurance Technology FAQ Blog Blog All Blog Posts Best Practices Careers Customer Viewpoint Developers General Interest Partner Perspective Technology Trends Industry Trends Industry Trends A Foundational Piece of Insurance Modernization You Can’t Afford to Overlook? Documents. When insurers talk about digital transformation, the conversation usually gravitates toward big, visible initiatives like core system replacements, cloud migration, or AI implementation. These are the headline investments that signal progress and ambition. In practice, transformation efforts can slow down or stall entirely for a much more grounded reason: documents. Not because any single document is especially difficult, but because there are thousands of them. Each form, policy, notice, endorsement, and invoice is tied to regulation, customer communication, and operational workflows. Individually manageable. Collectively overwhelming. This scale turns document management into a foundational piece of modernization that simply cannot be overlooked. The Hidden Complexity Behind Transformation Document generation sits at a uniquely challenging intersection within insurance organizations. It's neither just a technical function nor purely a business one. It connects compliance with customer experience, making it a critical touchpoint across the insurance lifecycle. Every document reflects a promise to the customer and a commitment to regulators. That's what can make document modernization so difficult. You're dealing with a deeply embedded layer of the business that touches everything else. Any change has ripple effects; a form update may impact multiple jurisdictions, downstream workflows, and customer touchpoints simultaneously. While transformation programs often focus on future-state capabilities, document management is rooted in present realities. Legacy formats, fragmented ownership, and regulatory requirements don't disappear when a new platform is introduced. They must be carefully resolved and that work is detailed and can be underestimated until it becomes the critical path. Why Documents Become the Bottleneck Documents can slow transformation, not because they are inherently complex, but because their complexity is layered and cumulative. First, there's sheer volume. Most insurers deal with thousands of documents. Each may have slight variations based on jurisdiction, product, or customer segment. Migrating that volume into a modern system requires rationalization, mapping, and validation at scale. "In my 32 years in the business, forms and compliance has always been the biggest headache.” -Karen Johnston, Vice President of Underwriting Operations at MEMIC Second, there's compliance weight. Unlike other system parts, documents are directly exposed to regulators and customers. Any errors can lead to regulatory penalties or eroded customer trust. This creates a natural tension where the business needs speed and agility, but every change must be auditable and defensible. Finally, there's the operating model itself. Historically, document changes have flowed through IT. The business identifies a need, submits a request, and waits for implementation. That model made sense when systems were tightly controlled and change was infrequent. But in today's environment of constant regulatory updates and product changes, it creates friction. The very structure of how work gets done becomes a constraint on progress. The Shift: From Bottleneck to Enabler What's changing now is both the technology used to manage documents and the way organizations think about them. One important shift is recognizing that much of this complexity is actually repeatable. In many lines of business, a large portion of document content is standardized across jurisdictions, with only a smaller percentage requiring localization. Once understood, it becomes possible to design systems around reuse rather than duplication. Instead of managing thousands of documents independently, organizations can create centralized libraries and templates. A single update can then be applied across multiple jurisdictions at once, dramatically reducing the effort required to stay compliant. What once required coordinated changes across dozens of variations can now be handled in a single, controlled update. Over time, this approach compounds efficiency gains and reduces operational risk. "Workers' comp forms are probably 80% standardized… so now if one of those forms changes, we can reflect that change across 47 jurisdictions all at once." -Karen Johnston, Vice President of Underwriting Operations at MEMIC Equally significant is the shift in ownership. Modern platforms enable business teams to take a more active role in managing documents, working alongside compliance and technology rather than routing every change through IT. This doesn't eliminate governance; it often strengthens it while changing who drives the process. The result is a more responsive organization. Instead of asking how long it will take to implement a change, the business can define the timeline based on need. IT still plays a critical role in maintaining the platform and ensuring stability, but it's no longer the bottleneck for every update. That shift unlocks speed and flexibility while creating closer alignment between business priorities and execution. Regulatory Requirements Up the Ante The urgency behind this shift is only increasing. Regulatory requirements continue to evolve with tighter timelines and greater scrutiny. Simultaneously, customers expect faster and more personalized communication. Documents have become a key part of the customer experience. Additionally, emerging technologies like AI depend on structured, well-managed content. Without a clean and consistent document foundation, it becomes much harder to automate processes or deliver intelligent communications. Document modernization is now more about enabling what comes next. Organizations that fail to address this layer risk undermining their broader transformation efforts. They may have modern core systems but still struggle to deliver updates quickly, maintain compliance efficiently, or provide expected customer communication levels. The bottleneck simply moves from one part of the organization to another. A Foundation for What’s Next For all the attention given to core platforms and new technologies, documents remain one of the most fundamental elements of insurance operations. They deliver policies and communicate claims, making them the most tangible output of the entire system. Document modernization plays a foundational role in transformation. When done well, it removes friction and creates a foundation for innovation. When overlooked, it quietly slows everything else down. The path to more agile, responsive insurance operations doesn't just run through new systems or technologies. It runs through the documents those systems produce and how effectively organizations can manage them at scale. Learn More To explore how insurers are applying these principles in practice, watch the episode of Marketplace Conversations I hosted featuring: Karen Johnston , Vice President of Underwriting Operations at MEMIC; Karl Lagasse , Vice President of Business Technology at MEMIC; and Angie Winn , Head of North America at GhostDraft. If we will look at lifeCycle of DoFn we will see the following Setup Repeatedly process bundles: StartBundle Repeated ProcessElement FinishBundle Teardown The service can be initialized in Setup or StartBundle but as I mentioned before I prefer to initialize it in the StartBundle lifeCycle because of the advantages of using the pipeline options inside the function. So because of that there is no way for Mockito to get the instance of the initialized service after the pipeline.run as we are initiating mocks before pipeline run and at that stage the service does not exist. So how can we overcome that problem ? The solution we found is not the proper Java way but it definitely works . Unlike in other projects we cannot use datadog agent in dataflow , therefore the only functionality supported by datadog in dataflows is metric collection and log collection. Because traces are not supported out of the box in dataflow we decided to implement them using the help of another service that is implementing ‘ dd-trace ’. So to achieve this we created a Singleton service that is initiating a dd tracer. The next step was to create two endpoints,one for starting and the second for closing active span, the only problem is that the active span object is not serializable , therefore it needs to be cached as an object in the service so later on it can be closed.
